name: FLORES-101
description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and professionally translated into 101 languages. The dataset covers a variety of topics and domains, with sentences sourced from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage. All translations are multilingually aligned, enabling evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems across 10,100 language pairs.
creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan (Facebook AI Research)
inLanguage: 101 languages including English, Spanish, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, and 94 others
citeAs: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan. 2021. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193v1 [cs.CL]
rai:dataCollection: Sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia, specifically from three sources: Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (age-appropriate nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guides). For each source, articles were selected at random, and 3-5 contiguous sentences were manually selected from each article, avoiding segments with very short or malformed sentences. Paragraphs were sampled equally from the beginning, middle, and end of articles. The selection process was performed by 10 annotators with different roles (researchers, engineers, program/project managers) from different regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, North America). For each sentence, metadata was extracted including Wikipedia URL, topic, and boolean flags indicating presence of entities and images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: English Wikipedia articles from three sources: Wikinews (collection of international news articles), Wikijunior (collection of age-appropriate nonfiction books for children from birth to age 12), and WikiVoyage (travel guide with articles about travel tips, food and destinations around the globe). One third of sentences were collected from each source.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage), and then manually selecting a few (typically between 3 and 5) contiguous sentences from each article, avoiding segments with very short or malformed sentences. To avoid bias from document structure, one paragraph per document was selected from either the beginning, middle or end of the article, with location selection balanced to be equally distributed across the whole corpus (roughly one third from beginning, one third from middle, one third from end). All sentences were manually labeled by sub-topic (one of 10 possibilities: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, and travel).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset construction involved professional translation rather than traditional annotation. For each of 101 target languages, all 3001 English source sentences were sent to Language Service Providers (LSPs) for translation. The translation workflow included: (1) translation by an initial LSP, (2) editing by different translators within the LSP, (3) automated quality control checks including language identification, checking for copied source sentences, length differences, fluency checks via language models, and detection of verbatim copies from commercial translation engines using sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU with specific thresholds (spBLEU > 50 for single engine, or spBLEU difference > 20 and spBLEU > 50 for multiple engines), (4) quality assurance by an independent LSP that provided a translation quality score (0-100 scale) based on identified errors (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register) with severity levels (minor, major, critical), and (5) re-translation if quality score was below 90% threshold. If initial score was below a certain threshold, re-translated versions received additional human evaluation. The process could repeat for multiple rounds until quality threshold was met. Any language with more than 10% of sentences violating the automatic copy-detection criteria required re-translation prior to human evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed through a Translation Quality Score calculated per language on a 0 to 100 scale, determined based on the number of identified errors by evaluation LSPs. Errors were examined across nine categories (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition or omission of information, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register), each associated with a severity level (minor, major, or critical). Evaluators were encouraged to pay particularly high attention to unnatural translation errors. The acceptable translation quality score threshold was set to 90%. The largest error category across all languages was mistranslation, which included incorrect interpretation of source text, literal translations, mistranslations of phrasal verbs, and lack of disambiguation of ambiguous terms. Error categories with few errors included register, grammar, and punctuation. Within languages, variation in error percentage by domain was observed (one domain could contribute up to 10% more errors than others), but across languages there was no clear trend indicating that all domains are challenging to translate.
rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators: 6 male and 4 female, with different roles in research (scientists, engineers, and program/project managers), originally coming from different regions of the world (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America and North America). Translation and quality assurance were performed by professional translators through Language Service Providers, though specific demographic information about these translators is not provided.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automated quality control checks were implemented including: (1) language identification tools, (2) checks for copied source sentences, (3) length difference checks, (4) language model-based fluency checks, and (5) sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU (spBLEU) comparison against outputs from commercial translation engines to detect verbatim copies.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that the potential to develop translation systems for languages all over the world is hindered by lack of reliable, high quality evaluation, and that without the fundamental ability to measure translation quality, it is impossible to develop, iterate, and test various models and techniques. They note that particularly for low-resource languages where there is little available training data, new methods and algorithms must be developed to improve translation. The majority of the world's population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages. The dataset enables evaluation of traditionally neglected regionally-relevant language pairs such as Xhosa-Zulu, Vietnamese-Thai, and Spanish-Aymara.
rai:dataBiases: The authors acknowledge that all source sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia, and that translating from English to other languages means that source sentences not in English are produced by human translators. They note that translationese (overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies, but conjecture that these effects are rather marginal when evaluating models in low-resource languages, where current MT systems produce many severe mistakes. They believe the benefits of many-to-many evaluation largely outsize the risk of evaluating translationese. The authors also note that while Wikipedia is supported in more than 260 languages, several low-resource languages have relatively few articles containing well structured sentences, which influenced their decision to source all sentences from English Wikipedia rather than from multiple language Wikipedias.
rai:dataLimitations: The authors note several limitations: (1) All source sentences are extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into other languages, meaning that source sentences not in English are produced by human translators rather than being naturally occurring text in those languages. This introduces translationese effects, though the authors argue these are marginal for low-resource language evaluation. (2) The dataset focuses on three specific domains (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage) which may not represent all possible use cases for machine translation. (3) Several low-resource languages have relatively few Wikipedia articles with well-structured sentences, which limited the ability to source sentences directly from those languages. (4) The sentence selection process involved only 10 annotators, all affiliated with the research lab, which may introduce some selection bias despite efforts to include annotators from diverse backgrounds and regions.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluation and testing of machine translation systems, particularly for low-resource and multilingual translation. Specific use cases include: (1) evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems across 10,100 language pairs, (2) evaluation of translation quality on the long tail of low-resource languages, (3) document-level translation evaluation (since multiple contiguous sentences from the same article are included with URLs), (4) multimodal machine translation evaluation (with metadata about images and hyperlinked entities), (5) comparison of direct many-to-many translation versus English-centric pivoting strategies, and (6) beyond translation, the dataset can be used to evaluate tasks such as sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation. The dataset is split into three portions: dev (for hyper-parameter tuning), devtest (for testing during development phase), and test (available only through evaluation server to prevent overfitting).
